_readme: Correct answer is always options[0] in this file, by design, to make authoring and verification easier. The app MUST shuffle option order at runtime before displaying a question, and recompute which shuffled index is correct. It must also randomly select 5 of the 10 questions per topic on each quiz attempt, without replacement within that attempt.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an element by index in an array?
questions.explanation: Arrays use direct index-based addressing, so lookup is constant time.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of an array of size n?
questions.explanation: All existing elements must shift right by one position.

questions.question: In a 0-indexed array of size n, what is the index of the last element?
questions.explanation: Indexing starts at 0, so the last valid index is n-1.

questions.question: Which approach checks if a string is a palindrome using only constant extra space?
options: Two pointers, one at each end, moving inward
Recursion that builds a new string each call
questions.explanation: Comparing characters from both ends inward needs no extra data structure.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of finding whether a target value exists in an unsorted array?
questions.explanation: Without ordering, every element may need to be checked.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of reversing a string in-place using two pointers?
questions.explanation: Only a constant number of extra variables are used.

questions.question: Which technique efficiently finds the maximum sum of a contiguous subarray of fixed size k?
questions.explanation: A window of size k slides across the array, updating the sum incrementally.

questions.question: Two strings are anagrams of each other if:
options: They contain the same characters with the same frequency, in any order
They have the same length only
They are palindromes of each other
They start with the same letter
questions.explanation: Order doesn't matter for anagrams, only character counts.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the classic Two Sum problem using a hash map?
questions.explanation: A single pass storing complements in a hash map achieves linear time.

questions.question: What does it mean for an array operation to be done "in-place"?
options: It uses only O(1) extra auxiliary space beyond the input
It creates a full copy of the array first
questions.explanation: In-place refers to space usage, not time complexity.

questions.question: The two-pointer technique is most naturally applied to:
options: Sorted arrays or sequences where relative order matters
questions.explanation: Ordering lets pointer movement reason about which side to shift.

questions.question: In finding a pair with a given sum on a sorted array, when the current sum is less than the target, what should you do?
questions.explanation: Moving left rightward increases the sum toward the target.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the two-pointer approach on a sorted array of size n to find a pair with a given sum?
questions.explanation: Each pointer moves at most n times total.

questions.question: Which of these is a classic two-pointer problem?
options: Removing duplicates from a sorted array
Finding the shortest path in a graph
questions.explanation: One pointer tracks the write position, another scans forward.

questions.question: In the "container with most water" problem, why move the pointer at the shorter line inward?
options: Because the shorter line limits the area, so only moving it could reveal a better answer
Because it reduces array size faster
Because it's always correct by definition
Because the taller line must always move first
questions.explanation: Moving the taller line inward can only decrease or keep area the same.

questions.question: What is the typical auxiliary space complexity of a two-pointer solution?
questions.explanation: Only a fixed number of pointer variables are needed.

questions.question: When merging two sorted arrays using two pointers, what determines the next element added to the result?
options: The smaller of the two current elements
The larger of the two current elements
questions.explanation: Taking the smaller element preserves sorted order in the merged result.

questions.question: The "fast and slow pointer" (tortoise and hare) technique is most commonly used to:
options: Detect a cycle in a linked list
questions.explanation: If a cycle exists, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow one.

questions.question: In the fast/slow pointer technique, how much faster does the fast pointer typically move?
questions.explanation: A 2:1 speed ratio is the standard formulation.

questions.question: What is a key precondition for using two pointers moving toward each other from opposite ends?
options: The array is typically sorted or has a relevant ordering property
The array must contain only unique elements
The array must have an even number of elements
The array must be a linked list
questions.explanation: Ordering is what makes inward movement meaningful.

questions.question: The sliding window technique is primarily used to:
options: Efficiently examine contiguous subarrays or substrings without recomputing from scratch
Traverse a tree level by level
Find the shortest path in a weighted graph
questions.explanation: The window updates incrementally as it slides.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of finding the maximum sum subarray of fixed size k using sliding window, on an array of size n?
questions.explanation: Each element enters and leaves the window exactly once.

questions.question: In a variable-size sliding window problem (e.g. smallest subarray with sum >= target), when does the window shrink from the left?
options: When the window already satisfies the condition and we want to minimize its size
When the right pointer reaches the end
questions.explanation: Shrinking while still valid helps find the minimum satisfying window.

questions.question: What data structure is often paired with sliding window to track character frequency?
options: A hash map (or fixed-size array for characters)
questions.explanation: Frequency counts are naturally tracked with a map or array.

questions.question: Sliding window is a good fit for a problem when it involves:
options: Contiguous sequences (subarrays/substrings) with a size or sum condition
Finding all permutations of a set
Finding the shortest path between two graph nodes
questions.explanation: Contiguity is the defining requirement for sliding window to apply.

questions.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of a basic fixed-size sliding window sum calculation?
questions.explanation: Only the running sum and window bounds need to be stored.

questions.question: In "longest substring without repeating characters," what triggers shrinking the window from the left?
options: Encountering a character already present in the current window
Reaching the end of the string
The window size exceeding the string's length
questions.explanation: A repeat means the window must shrink until the duplicate is removed.

questions.question: Compared to a brute-force nested-loop approach for subarray problems, sliding window typically improves time complexity from:
questions.explanation: Sliding window avoids recomputing overlapping work across subarrays.

questions.question: For "maximum sum subarray of size k," what does each slide of the window do to the running sum?
options: Subtract the element leaving and add the element entering
Recompute the entire sum from scratch
Multiply the sum by the window size
questions.explanation: This incremental update is what makes sliding window O(n).

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a typical sliding window problem?
options: Finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph (BFS)
Longest substring with at most k distinct characters
Maximum sum subarray of size k
Minimum size subarray with sum >= target
questions.explanation: BFS shortest path is a graph traversal problem, unrelated to contiguous windows.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting a node at the head of a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Only the head pointer needs updating.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing the k-th element of a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Linked lists require sequential traversal from the head.

questions.question: To reverse a singly linked list iteratively, what three pointers are typically tracked?
questions.explanation: These three pointers let you rewire each node's next pointer safely.

questions.question: How does the fast/slow pointer technique find the middle of a linked list?
options: Slow moves one step, fast moves two; when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle
Both pointers move at the same speed and stop together
The fast pointer moves backward while slow moves forward
It requires knowing the list's length in advance
questions.explanation: The 2:1 speed ratio naturally lands slow at the midpoint.

questions.question: What is a key difference between a singly linked list and a doubly linked list?
options: A doubly linked list has pointers to both the next and previous nodes
A singly linked list can be traversed backward easily
A doubly linked list cannot be traversed forward
questions.explanation: The extra previous pointer enables backward traversal.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of reversing a linked list iteratively (no recursion)?
questions.explanation: Only a few pointer variables are used, regardless of list length.

questions.question: In Floyd's cycle detection, if a cycle exists, what eventually happens?
options: The fast and slow pointers meet at some node inside the cycle
Both pointers reach null at the same time
The slow pointer overtakes the fast pointer
questions.explanation: Inside a cycle, the faster pointer eventually catches up to the slower one.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of deleting a node from the middle of a singly linked list, given a pointer to the node before it?
questions.explanation: Only pointer reassignment is needed once you have the preceding node.

questions.question: Why can't you efficiently binary search a singly linked list the way you would an array?
options: You cannot access an arbitrary middle element in O(1) time — you must traverse to it
Binary search requires a doubly linked list
It is possible and equally efficient
questions.explanation: Lack of random access removes binary search's core advantage.

questions.question: What does it mean when a linked list node's "next" pointer is null?
options: It marks the end of the list
It means the list is empty
It means the node is the head
questions.explanation: A null next pointer signals there are no further nodes.

questions.question: A stack follows which ordering principle?
questions.explanation: The most recently pushed element is the first to be popped.

questions.question: A queue follows which ordering principle?
questions.explanation: Elements are removed in the same order they were added.

questions.question: What is the amortized time complexity of push and pop on a stack backed by a dynamic array?
questions.explanation: Occasional resizing is amortized across many operations.

questions.question: Which classic problem is commonly solved using a stack?
options: Checking for balanced parentheses in an expression
Finding the shortest path in a graph
Finding the median of a data stream
questions.explanation: Matching brackets naturally fits a last-in-first-out structure.

questions.question: How can a queue be implemented using two stacks?
options: Push onto one stack; move elements to a second stack (reversing order) when dequeuing
Use a single stack directly for both operations
It's not possible with only stacks
Use two stacks that always mirror each other
questions.explanation: The double reversal across two stacks restores FIFO order.

questions.question: What is a "monotonic stack" typically used for?
options: Efficiently finding the next greater or smaller element for each item in an array
Sorting an array in O(n log n)
Detecting cycles in a linked list
questions.explanation: Maintaining increasing or decreasing order on the stack helps answer these queries in linear time.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of enqueue and dequeue in a properly implemented circular queue?
questions.explanation: Both operations just move front/rear indices.

questions.question: In a call stack used for recursive function calls, what happens when a function returns?
options: Its stack frame is popped off the top of the stack
A new stack frame is pushed
questions.explanation: Returning removes that function's frame, resuming the caller.

questions.question: Which data structure would you use to implement an "undo" feature in a text editor?
questions.explanation: The most recent action should be the first one undone.

questions.question: What is a common use case for a queue in breadth-first search (BFS)?
options: Processing nodes level by level in the order they were discovered
Processing nodes in reverse order of discovery
questions.explanation: FIFO order matches BFS's level-by-level expansion.

questions.question: In a binary search tree (BST), for any node, all values in the left subtree are:
questions.explanation: This ordering property is what defines a BST.

questions.question: What is the average-case time complexity of search, insert, and delete in a balanced BST?
questions.explanation: Balance keeps the tree's height logarithmic in the number of nodes.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of search in an unbalanced (skewed) BST?
questions.explanation: A skewed BST degenerates into a structure similar to a linked list.

questions.question: Which traversal visits nodes in the order: left subtree, root, right subtree?
questions.explanation: This is the definition of in-order traversal.

questions.question: Which traversal visits the root before its children?
questions.explanation: Pre-order visits root, then left, then right.

questions.question: What does an in-order traversal of a valid binary search tree produce?
options: The node values in sorted (ascending) order
The node values in reverse sorted order
The tree's height at each node
questions.explanation: The BST ordering property guarantees sorted output from in-order traversal.

questions.question: What data structure is typically used to implement a level-order (breadth-first) tree traversal?
questions.explanation: FIFO order matches processing nodes level by level.

questions.question: In a self-balancing tree like an AVL tree, what is maintained to keep operations efficient?
options: The height difference between left and right subtrees stays small
All leaf nodes are at exactly the same depth always
The tree becomes a perfect binary tree
Nodes are stored in a plain array
questions.explanation: Bounded height difference keeps operations logarithmic.

questions.question: What is the maximum number of children a node can have in a binary tree?
questions.explanation: "Binary" specifically means at most two children per node.

questions.question: What is a "leaf node" in a tree?
options: The root node of the tree
A node with exactly one child
A node with the maximum value in the tree
questions.explanation: Leaves are the terminal nodes at the bottom of the tree.

questions.question: Which traversal algorithm uses a queue and explores a graph level by level?
questions.explanation: BFS expands outward one level at a time using a queue.

questions.question: Which traversal typically uses a stack (or recursion) and explores as far as possible along one branch before backtracking?
questions.explanation: DFS commits to a path and backtracks only when it hits a dead end.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of BFS or DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges, using an adjacency list?
questions.explanation: Each vertex and edge is processed a constant number of times.

questions.question: Which algorithm is commonly used to find the shortest path in a graph with non-negative edge weights?
questions.explanation: Dijkstra's greedily expands the nearest unvisited node.

questions.question: What does it mean for a graph to be "directed"?
options: Edges have a specific direction from one vertex to another
All edges must form a cycle
Every vertex connects to every other vertex
questions.explanation: Directed edges represent a one-way relationship between vertices.

questions.question: What is a common way to represent a sparse graph (relatively few edges) in code?
options: A single array of all vertices
questions.explanation: Adjacency lists avoid wasting space on non-existent edges.

questions.question: What does BFS naturally find in an unweighted graph, starting from a source node?
options: The shortest path (fewest edges) to every reachable node
The longest path in the graph
questions.explanation: BFS's level-by-level expansion guarantees shortest-edge-count paths.

questions.question: What technique detects a cycle in a directed graph during DFS?
options: Tracking nodes currently in the recursion stack and checking if one is revisited
Counting the total number of edges
Using a queue instead of a stack
questions.explanation: Revisiting a node still "in progress" on the current path indicates a cycle.

questions.question: A "topological sort" is applicable to:
options: A graph with negative weight cycles
questions.explanation: Topological order requires a consistent direction with no cycles.

questions.question: In an undirected graph, how many directions does a single edge between two vertices represent?
options: Only from the first vertex to the second
Only from the second vertex to the first
questions.explanation: Undirected edges have no inherent direction.

questions.question: Every recursive function must have what to avoid infinite recursion?
options: A base case that stops further recursive calls
questions.explanation: The base case is what eventually halts the recursive chain.

questions.question: What data structure implicitly manages recursive function calls "under the hood"?
questions.explanation: Each call pushes a new frame; returning pops it.

questions.question: What is "backtracking" primarily used for?
options: Exploring all possible solutions incrementally and abandoning ones that fail constraints
Finding the shortest path in a weighted graph
questions.explanation: Backtracking systematically builds and discards candidate solutions.

questions.question: In backtracking, what happens when a partial solution violates a constraint?
options: The algorithm undoes the last choice and tries a different option
The algorithm terminates immediately with no answer
The algorithm ignores the constraint and continues
The algorithm restarts from scratch with new input
questions.explanation: Undoing the last choice is the "backtrack" step.

questions.question: Which classic problem is commonly solved using backtracking?
options: Finding the maximum element in an array
questions.explanation: N-Queens requires exploring and undoing placements that violate constraints.

questions.question: What is a risk of recursion without a well-designed base case or with excessive depth?
questions.explanation: Each call consumes stack space; too many unresolved calls overflow it.

questions.question: What is "memoization" used for in recursive algorithms?
options: Caching results of expensive function calls to avoid redundant recomputation
Converting recursion into a loop automatically
questions.explanation: Cached results skip recomputing already-solved subproblems.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of naive (non-memoized) recursive computation of the n-th Fibonacci number?
questions.explanation: The same subproblems are recomputed repeatedly, causing exponential growth.

questions.question: What does "pruning" mean in backtracking algorithms?
options: Stopping exploration of a branch early once it can't lead to a valid solution
questions.explanation: Pruning avoids wasting time on branches that are already known to fail.

questions.question: A recursive function that calls itself directly is described as:
questions.explanation: Direct recursion means the function invokes itself, not another function that calls it back.

questions.question: Dynamic programming is most effective on problems that exhibit:
options: Completely independent subproblems with no repetition
Only a single possible solution path
questions.explanation: These two properties are the defining conditions for DP to help.

questions.question: What is "optimal substructure" in dynamic programming?
options: An optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions to its subproblems
Every subproblem must be solved randomly
The problem has no smaller subproblems
questions.explanation: This property lets DP combine subproblem solutions into the overall answer.

questions.question: What is the key difference between top-down (memoization) and bottom-up (tabulation) DP?
options: Top-down uses recursion with caching; bottom-up builds iteratively from smaller subproblems upward
Bottom-up cannot be used for optimization problems
questions.explanation: Both avoid recomputation, just via different control flow.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of computing the n-th Fibonacci number using DP (memoization or tabulation)?
questions.explanation: Each of the n subproblems is solved exactly once.

questions.question: In the classic 0/1 Knapsack problem, what does "0/1" refer to?
options: Each item can be fully included or excluded — no fractional or repeated inclusion
Only 0 or 1 items total can be chosen
The knapsack has exactly one compartment
Items can be split into fractions
questions.explanation: The 0/1 naming reflects the binary include/exclude choice per item.

questions.question: What is memoization primarily trying to avoid?
options: Redundant recomputation of the same subproblem multiple times
questions.explanation: Caching prior results is exactly what prevents repeat work.

questions.question: In the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem, what does dp[i][j] typically represent?
options: The length of the LCS of the first i characters of one string and the first j of the other
The total length of both strings
The edit distance between the strings
questions.explanation: This is the standard state definition for the LCS DP table.

questions.question: Compared to a naive exponential recursive solution, what does DP typically trade to achieve better time complexity?
options: Additional space to store previously computed subproblem results
The need for a base case
questions.explanation: This is the classic time-space tradeoff DP relies on.

questions.question: Which of these is a classic dynamic programming problem?
options: Coin change (minimum coins to make a given amount)
Binary search in a sorted array
questions.explanation: Coin change has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.

questions.question: What does "state" typically refer to in a dynamic programming solution?
options: The specific combination of parameters that uniquely defines a subproblem
questions.explanation: State is what indexes each entry in a DP table or memo.

questions.question: A greedy algorithm makes decisions based on:
options: The locally optimal choice at each step, hoping it leads to a global optimum
Always looking many steps ahead before deciding
questions.explanation: This is the defining behavior of a greedy strategy.

questions.question: Does a greedy algorithm always guarantee the globally optimal solution?
options: No — only for problems with the "greedy choice property"
Yes, but only for sorting problems
questions.explanation: Greedy correctness depends on the specific problem's structure.

questions.question: Which problem is efficiently solved by a greedy approach in standard currency systems?
options: The coin change problem with standard denominations
Finding the longest path in a general graph
questions.explanation: Standard denominations happen to satisfy the greedy choice property.

questions.question: In the activity selection problem, what greedy strategy is typically used?
options: Always pick the remaining activity that finishes earliest
Always pick the activity that starts earliest, regardless of finish time
questions.explanation: Earliest finish time leaves the most room for future activities.

questions.question: What key characteristic makes a problem suitable for a greedy algorithm?
options: The greedy choice property and optimal substructure
Requiring exhaustive search of all combinations
Having no clear ordering of choices
questions.explanation: Both properties together justify making locally optimal choices.

questions.question: Which of these is a classic greedy algorithm?
options: Kruskal's algorithm for minimum spanning tree
Dynamic programming for the knapsack problem
questions.explanation: Kruskal's repeatedly picks the smallest edge that doesn't form a cycle.

questions.question: Why does the fractional knapsack problem work well with a greedy approach, unlike 0/1 knapsack?
options: You can take the highest value-to-weight items first, filling remaining capacity with a fraction of the next item
0/1 knapsack always has a valid greedy solution too
Greedy only works on sorted arrays in general
questions.explanation: Divisibility removes the all-or-nothing constraint that breaks greedy for 0/1 knapsack.

questions.question: Huffman coding, used for data compression, is an example of which algorithmic strategy?
questions.explanation: Huffman coding greedily merges the two lowest-frequency nodes at each step.

questions.question: What is a common risk of applying a greedy algorithm to a problem without the greedy choice property?
options: It may produce a locally optimal but globally suboptimal result
It will always take exponential time
It will always be slower than brute force
questions.explanation: Greedy can silently return a wrong answer if the property doesn't hold.

questions.question: In Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm, what greedy choice is made at each step?
options: Expand the unvisited node with the currently smallest known distance from the source
Expand the node with the largest distance
questions.explanation: This choice guarantees correctness when edge weights are non-negative.

questions.question: What is the average-case time complexity of QuickSort?
questions.explanation: Balanced partitions on average yield log n levels of n work each.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of QuickSort?
questions.explanation: Poor pivot choices (e.g. already-sorted input with a naive pivot) cause unbalanced partitions.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of MergeSort in all cases (best, average, worst)?
questions.explanation: Merge sort's divide-and-conquer structure is consistent regardless of input order.

questions.question: What is a precondition for performing binary search on a dataset?
options: The data must be a linked list
The data must contain only unique elements
The data must be an array of size 2^k
questions.explanation: Binary search relies on being able to discard half the remaining range based on order.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of size n?
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the remaining search space.

questions.question: Which sorting algorithm is "stable," meaning equal elements retain their relative order?
questions.explanation: Merge sort's merge step preserves the original relative order of equal elements.

questions.question: What is the space complexity of a typical array-based MergeSort implementation?
questions.explanation: Merging sorted halves typically requires auxiliary arrays.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of building a heap from an unsorted array (heapify)?
questions.explanation: A bottom-up heapify does less work than repeatedly inserting one at a time.

questions.question: In binary search, after comparing the target to the middle element, what happens if the target is smaller?
options: The search continues in the left half, discarding the right half
The search continues in the right half
questions.explanation: Discarding the half that can't contain the target is the core of binary search.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of Bubble Sort in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Nested comparisons across the array give quadratic worst-case time.

questions.question: What does the bitwise AND operator (&) return when applied to two bits?
questions.explanation: AND requires both operand bits to be 1 to produce 1.

questions.question: What does the bitwise XOR operator (^) return when applied to two identical bits?
questions.explanation: XOR returns 0 whenever both bits match.

questions.question: How does XOR help solve the "single number" problem (one element appears once, all others twice)?
options: XOR-ing all elements together cancels out pairs, leaving only the unique element
XOR always returns the largest element
XOR is used to count elements
questions.explanation: A number XORed with itself is 0, so paired duplicates cancel out.

questions.question: What does a left shift operation (x << 1) do to an integer x?
questions.explanation: Shifting bits left by one is equivalent to multiplying by 2.

questions.question: What does a right shift operation (x >> 1) do to a positive integer x?
questions.explanation: Shifting bits right by one is equivalent to integer division by 2.

questions.question: How can you check if an integer is even or odd using bitwise operations?
options: Check if the last bit (x & 1) is 0 (even) or 1 (odd)
Check if x is greater than 0
questions.explanation: The lowest bit directly encodes parity in binary representation.

questions.question: What is a common bit trick to check if a positive integer is a power of two?
options: Check if x is divisible by 3
Right shift x until it equals 1, which always works with no exceptions
questions.explanation: Powers of two have exactly one set bit, which this trick exploits.

questions.question: What does the bitwise NOT operator (~) do to a bit?
questions.explanation: NOT inverts every bit of its operand.

questions.question: How many bits are typically used to represent a standard 32-bit signed integer?
questions.explanation: This is the defining width of a 32-bit integer type.

questions.question: What is a common technique to count the number of set bits (1s) in an integer?
options: Repeatedly clear the lowest set bit using x & (x - 1), counting iterations
Divide the number by 2 repeatedly and sum the results
Convert to a string and count characters only
It cannot be done without a lookup table
questions.explanation: Brian Kernighan's technique clears one set bit per iteration, giving an O(set bits) count.
